theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What core temperature should the thickest part of cooked chicken reach, checked with a clean probe thermometer (or as the Centre's food safety plan says)?
options: About 54 °C
About 63 °C
About 74 °C
About 100 °C

questions.stem: Which bacteria are most often carried by raw chicken?
options: Salmonella and Campylobacter
Yeast and bread moulds

Lactic acid and yoghurt cultures

questions.stem: Where should raw chicken be kept in a fridge?

Beside the cooked rice, to save space
In the door shelf, so it is easy to reach

questions.stem: A probe thermometer is checked by putting it in iced water. About what should it read?
At what temperature should cooked chicken be kept hot for service (or as the Centre's food safety plan says)?

About 45 °C or above

questions.stem: Jerk chicken is traditionally cooked:

questions.stem: Why do cooks weigh chicken portions?

questions.stem: Which is the best way to present brown stew chicken for service?

options: Wash with hot detergent water, then sanitise it

options: Cooking chicken to 74 °C and serving it at once
Using one board for raw chicken, then salad
Storing cooked rice in a covered container

questions.stem: How should leftover cooked chicken be stored in the fridge?
options: Left uncovered, so steam can escape
On the bottom shelf, under the raw meat
Covered, labelled, dated, above raw meat
In the pot it was cooked in, with a lid

essays.stem: Explain how you would stop cross-contamination when you prepare raw chicken and a salad in the same kitchen.
essays.modelAnswer: Cross-contamination is when bacteria pass from raw food to food that will not be cooked again. First, I wash my hands well before I start. I prepare the salad first, or in a separate area, and keep it covered in the fridge. I use a separate board and knife for raw chicken, using the colour the Centre's colour code gives for raw poultry, and a green board for salad. I do not rinse the chicken under the tap, because splashes spread bacteria. After the chicken, I wash my hands again and clean and sanitise the board, knife and bench. In the fridge, raw chicken goes in a covered tray on the bottom shelf, below the salad and cooked food. I use clean cloths and change them often, and I never use the same tongs for raw and cooked chicken.
markingPoints: Separate boards and knives for raw chicken and salad (colour-coded if the Centre uses them)
Hand washing before and after handling raw chicken
Clean and sanitise boards, knives and surfaces after raw chicken
Raw chicken stored covered on the bottom shelf, below ready-to-eat food
Separate utensils for raw and cooked; clean cloths; no rinsing chicken under the tap

essays.stem: Describe how you would receive, store and thaw a delivery of frozen chicken safely.
essays.modelAnswer: When the delivery comes, I check it straight away. The chicken should be frozen hard, with the packaging whole and not torn, and no signs of thawing or freezer burn. I check the use-by date and the supplier's details, and I can check the temperature with a probe between two packs. If it is not right, I tell the supervisor and it is sent back. I put it into the freezer quickly, at -18 °C or below, labelled with the date, and I put new stock behind old stock (first in, first out). To thaw, I put the chicken in a tray on the bottom shelf of the fridge, covered and labelled, so drips cannot fall on other food. A whole chicken can take a day or more. It is fully thawed when there is no ice in the cavity and the legs move freely. I never thaw chicken on the counter or in warm water, and I cook it soon after it has thawed.
markingPoints: Check the delivery: frozen hard, packaging whole, dates, reject if not right
Store quickly in the freezer at -18 °C or below, labelled and dated
First in, first out stock rotation
Thaw in the fridge, in a covered tray on the bottom shelf; never on the counter or in warm water
Check it is fully thawed (no ice, legs move freely) and cook it soon after

essays.stem: Describe the steps to joint a whole chicken into 8 pieces.
essays.modelAnswer: I set a clean board on a damp cloth so it cannot slip, use the board the Centre's colour code gives for raw poultry, and use a sharp boning knife or cook's knife. I take out the giblets and pat the bird dry with kitchen paper. I lay the chicken on its back. I pull a leg away from the body, cut through the skin, and bend the leg back until the thigh joint pops out, then cut through the joint to take off the leg. I do the same on the other side. I cut each leg at the joint between the thigh and the drumstick, which gives 4 pieces. Next I cut off each wing at the joint. Then I cut along the breastbone and down through the rib cage to take off each breast, and I cut each breast in half across. That gives 2 drumsticks, 2 thighs, 2 wings and 2 breast pieces. The back and bones are kept for stock. I wash my hands and clean and sanitise the board and knife afterwards.
markingPoints: Safe set-up: correct board on a damp cloth, sharp suitable knife, giblets out
Legs removed through the hip joint, then split at the knee into thigh and drumstick
Wings removed at the joint
Breasts removed along the breastbone and cut to give the right pieces
Carcass kept for stock; hands, board and knife cleaned and sanitised

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare, marinate and cook jerk chicken safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I make the jerk seasoning by blending Scotch bonnet peppers, scallion, thyme, pimento (allspice), garlic, ginger, black pepper, salt, a little sugar and some vinegar or lime juice. I wear disposable gloves when cutting the peppers, and I do not touch my eyes. I cut the chicken into quarters and score the thick parts so the seasoning goes in. I rub the seasoning all over, put the chicken in a covered, labelled container and leave it in the fridge to marinate, best overnight. I cook it slowly on a grill over pimento wood or charcoal, or in an oven, turning it so it browns but does not burn. I check the thickest part with a clean probe thermometer: it must reach about 74 °C (or as the Centre's plan says). I use clean tongs for the cooked chicken, not the ones used for raw. Any marinade left over is thrown away or boiled. I chop the chicken and serve it hot with festival or hard-dough bread.
markingPoints: Jerk seasoning ingredients: Scotch bonnet, pimento, scallion, thyme and others
Gloves for the peppers; do not touch the eyes
Marinate covered and labelled in the fridge, never at room temperature
Cook slowly over pimento wood, charcoal or in the oven, turning so it does not burn
Core temperature about 74 °C checked with a clean probe; separate tongs; leftover raw marinade not reused unless boiled

essays.stem: Describe the method for cooking brown stew chicken, from seasoning to serving.
essays.modelAnswer: I cut the chicken into pieces and trim off extra fat. I season it with salt, black pepper, garlic, thyme, scallion, onion and a little browning, and leave it covered in the fridge to take on the flavour. When I am ready to cook, I shake off the herbs and onion and keep them. I heat oil in a heavy pot and brown the chicken pieces well on all sides, a few at a time so the oil stays hot. I take out the chicken, then soften the onion, sweet pepper, tomato and herbs in the pot. I put the chicken back with a little water or stock and some ketchup if the recipe says so. I cover the pot and stew it gently for about 30 to 40 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender and the gravy is thick. I check the core temperature with a clean probe (about 74 °C). I taste the gravy with a clean spoon and adjust the seasoning, then serve it hot on a warm plate with rice and peas.
markingPoints: Season the chicken and leave it covered in the fridge
Brown the pieces well in hot oil, a few at a time
Soften onion, peppers, tomato and herbs, then return the chicken with a little liquid
Cover and stew gently until tender, with a thick gravy
Check the core temperature, taste with a clean spoon and serve hot

essays.stem: Explain how to check that chicken is fully cooked, and how to use and look after a probe thermometer.
essays.modelAnswer: Chicken can carry bacteria such as Salmonella, so it must be cooked right through. The safe check is the core temperature. I clean and sanitise the probe, then push it into the thickest part of the piece, such as the thigh, without touching the bone, because bone gives a false reading. I wait until the reading stops moving. It should reach about 74 °C, or the figure in the Centre's food safety plan. I also look for juices that run clear and no pink flesh near the bone, but I do not trust colour alone. I write the temperature on the temperature log. After each use I clean and sanitise the probe, so I do not carry bacteria from raw or part-cooked food to cooked food. I check that the probe is accurate as the Centre says, for example in iced water (about 0 °C) and boiling water (about 100 °C). If it is wrong, I tell the supervisor and do not use it. I keep the probe in its case and change the battery when it is low.
markingPoints: Probe in the thickest part, not touching bone; wait for a steady reading
Core temperature about 74 °C (or as the Centre's plan says)
Colour and clear juices are signs only, not proof
Clean and sanitise the probe before and after each use; record the temperature
Check the probe's accuracy (iced and boiling water), report faults, store it safely

essays.stem: Compare roasting and stewing as ways of cooking chicken. Say which birds or cuts suit each method, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Roasting is a dry heat method. The chicken cooks in a hot oven with a little fat, and is basted now and then. It gives crisp brown skin and a good flavour. Roasting suits young, tender birds such as broilers or spring chickens, and whole birds or leg quarters. It is not good for old, tough birds, because dry heat does not soften them. Stewing is a moist heat method. The chicken is cut into pieces and cooked slowly in a covered pot with liquid, vegetables and seasoning, as in brown stew chicken or curry chicken. Slow, moist cooking softens tougher meat, so stewing suits older birds such as a boiling fowl, and cuts like thighs, drumsticks and backs. The liquid becomes a tasty gravy that is served with the chicken. Both methods must bring the chicken to a core temperature of about 74 °C. Roasting needs care so the breast does not dry out; stewing needs a gentle heat so the meat does not break up.
markingPoints: Roasting is dry heat in an oven: crisp brown skin
Roasting suits young tender birds and whole birds or quarters
Stewing is slow moist heat in a covered pot with liquid
Stewing suits older or tougher birds and cuts; makes a gravy
Both reach a safe core temperature; care points (breast drying out, gentle simmer)

essays.stem: Describe how to deep fry chicken pieces safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the fryer is clean, that the oil is fresh and filled to the mark, and that a fire blanket and the right extinguisher are near. I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules. I heat the oil to about 160–180 °C. I pat the chicken dry or let the extra batter drip off, because water makes hot oil spit. I fry small batches so the oil stays hot and does not overflow. I lower the basket slowly, or lay the pieces in away from me, never dropping them in. I never leave the fryer while it is on. I cook the chicken until it is golden and the core reaches about 74 °C, checked with a clean probe. I lift the basket, let it drain, and put the chicken on kitchen paper. If the oil catches fire, I turn off the heat and cover it with a fire blanket, and never use water. When I finish, I switch off and let the oil cool before filtering or changing it.
markingPoints: Check the fryer, oil level and fire equipment before use; follow the maker's instructions
Oil at about 160–180 °C; dry food and small batches
Lower food in slowly, away from the body; never leave the fryer
Core temperature about 74 °C checked with a probe; drain the chicken
Oil fire: heat off and fire blanket, never water; let oil cool before handling

essays.stem: Explain how cooked chicken should be kept hot, cooled and reheated safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Bacteria grow fastest in the danger zone, between 5 °C and 63 °C, so cooked chicken must not stay there long. To keep it hot for service, I hold it at about 63 °C or above in a bain-marie or hot cupboard and check it with a probe, writing the readings on the log. If chicken is to be kept for later, I cool it quickly: I spread it out in shallow trays, or stand the container in iced water, and put it in the fridge, covered, as soon as it has cooled, within the time the Centre's food safety plan gives. I label it with the name and date and store it above raw food, at 5 °C or below. To reheat, I heat it until the core reaches about 74 °C, checked with a clean probe, and I reheat it once only. Any chicken that has been reheated and is left over is thrown away.
markingPoints: Explains the danger zone (5 °C to 63 °C)
Hot-hold at about 63 °C or above, checked and recorded
Cool quickly in shallow trays or an ice bath, then refrigerate covered at 5 °C or below
Label and date; store above raw food
Reheat to about 74 °C core, once only; throw away reheated leftovers

essays.stem: Describe how you would check the quality of a finished poultry dish and present it for service.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check that the chicken is safe: the core temperature has reached about 74 °C with a clean probe. Then I check the quality. The chicken should be tender and moist, not dry or tough, and the skin or coating should be an even golden brown, not burnt. The sauce or gravy should be the right thickness and colour. I taste the sauce with a clean spoon, never with my fingers, and adjust the seasoning. I check the portion is the size in the standard recipe. To present it, I use a clean, warm plate. I place the chicken neatly, add the sauce so it does not run over the rim, and add the side dishes, such as rice and peas and steamed vegetables. I add a simple garnish, such as chopped scallion or a sprig of thyme. I wipe the rim with a clean cloth and send the plate out quickly, so it reaches the guest hot.
markingPoints: Safety check: core temperature about 74 °C
Quality checks: tender, moist, even colour, right sauce thickness
Taste with a clean spoon and adjust the seasoning; correct portion size
Clean warm plate, neat placing, suitable garnish, clean rim
Served quickly so it reaches the guest hot

practical1.title: Joint whole chickens and cook brown stew chicken
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare and cook brown stew chicken for 8 portions. Set up a safe raw-poultry work area first. Each member joints one whole chicken (or, for a group of 5, the assessor gives the fifth member two halves) into 8 pieces with the assessor watching, and keeps the backs and necks for stock. Together, season the chicken and keep it covered in the fridge until it is time to cook. Each member takes a turn browning a batch of chicken in the pot, and every member checks and records the core temperature of at least one piece with a clean probe thermometer. Stew the chicken until tender, taste and adjust the seasoning, and plate 4 portions with rice and a garnish. Then clean and sanitise the whole area. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the plates are done and the area is clean.
materials: 4 or 5 whole chickens (about 1.4–1.6 kg each), thawed in the fridge
Seasoning: onion, garlic, scallion, thyme, sweet pepper, tomato, salt, black pepper, browning
Vegetable oil, and water or stock
Boning knives or cook's knives, chopping boards in the Centre's colour for raw poultry
Heavy-based pot with lid, tongs, trays, covered containers, labels
Clean probe thermometer, probe wipes, temperature log sheet
Detergent, food-safe sanitiser, clean cloths, disposable gloves
photos: The raw-poultry work area set up, boards on damp cloths, every member in a clean uniform and hairnet
Each member's chicken jointed into 8 pieces on the board
The seasoned chicken in a covered, labelled container in the fridge
A batch of chicken being browned in the pot
The probe in the thickest piece, showing the reading, and the completed temperature log
4 finished plates of brown stew chicken with rice and garnish
The work area cleaned and sanitised, knives clean and put away
checklist: Washed hands and wore a clean uniform, apron and hair cover; no jewellery
Used the right board on a damp cloth, and a sharp suitable knife held safely
Jointed the chicken into 8 neat pieces through the joints
Kept raw chicken apart from cooked and ready-to-eat food, and did not rinse it under the tap
Browned the chicken safely in hot oil, laying pieces in away from the body
Checked the core temperature (about 74 °C) with a clean probe and recorded it
Tasted with a clean spoon and plated neatly on a warm plate with a clean rim
Cleaned and sanitised boards, knives, surfaces and equipment, and put waste in the right bin
safety: Carry knives point down by your side, and never try to catch a falling knife
Keep raw chicken on its own board and area; wash your hands after touching it
Turn pan handles inwards and use dry oven cloths for hot pots
Keep a fire blanket near the stove; never put water on burning oil
Mop up spills straight away and put out a wet-floor sign

practical2.title: Make jerk seasoning, cook jerk chicken quarters and roast a trussed chicken
practical2.brief: As a group, make a batch of jerk seasoning, then cook jerk chicken and a whole roast chicken. The assessor gives you chicken leg quarters and two whole chickens. Every member helps to cut and weigh the seasoning ingredients, wearing gloves for the Scotch bonnet peppers, and the group blends the seasoning. Each member scores and seasons at least two leg quarters, which marinate covered and labelled in the fridge for at least 1 hour (or the assessor gives a batch marinated the day before). Two members truss one whole chicken each, with the others helping, and the group roasts them, basting now and then. Cook the jerk chicken on the grill or in the oven. Each member checks and records the core temperature of at least one piece, rests and carves or chops the chicken, and plates one portion. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the plates are done and the area is clean.
materials: 8–10 chicken leg quarters and 2 whole chickens, thawed in the fridge
Jerk seasoning: Scotch bonnet peppers, scallion, thyme, pimento (allspice), garlic, ginger, black pepper, salt, sugar, vinegar or lime juice
Blender or food processor with its guard and lid
Disposable gloves, chopping boards in the Centre's colour code, knives
Trussing needle and string, roasting trays, grill or oven
Clean probe thermometer, probe wipes, temperature log sheet
Festival or hard-dough bread to serve; plates
photos: The seasoning ingredients weighed and cut, with gloves worn for the peppers
The finished jerk seasoning, and the scored chicken being seasoned
The seasoned chicken covered and labelled in the fridge
Each whole chicken trussed, before roasting
The chicken on the grill or in the oven
The probe in the thickest part of a piece, with the reading, and the completed temperature log
The finished plates of jerk chicken and roast chicken
The work area cleaned and sanitised at the end
checklist: Wore gloves for the peppers and did not touch the face or eyes
Made and used the seasoning as the recipe says, weighing the ingredients
Marinated the chicken covered and labelled in the fridge, not at room temperature
Trussed or helped to truss a chicken neatly so it holds its shape
Cooked and turned the chicken safely so it browned evenly without burning
Checked the core temperature (about 74 °C) with a clean probe and recorded it
Used separate tongs and boards for raw and cooked chicken
Rested, carved or chopped and plated a neat portion, then cleaned the area
safety: Fit the blender lid and guard before switching on, and unplug it before cleaning
Wash your hands after handling hot peppers, even when gloves were worn
Use dry oven cloths for hot trays, and warn others when carrying them
Keep the grill area clear, and keep a fire blanket and extinguisher near
Throw away any raw marinade left over; never put it on cooked food
